latin.372: PLAC. Forte cum separabilia dicis, intelligis non modo separari posse, ita ut scilicet, amissis honoribus, remanere possint divitiae, & amissa nobilitate, remanere possint affinitates. Quod si ita explicatur, quis non regerat, & bona Adami fuisse separabilia, quia & lumen naturale intellectus, & communes notiones, & opus legis scriptum in cordibus remanere potuit, & amitti tamen rectitudo, justitia, sanctitas — & factum esse novimus. Et in hoc iterum similitudo constat. At ubi dissimilitudinis capita explicantur, de primo membro nihil dicitur? Agnosco non ita quatuor membra a me proposita, ut non quatenus ordine singula explicata sint, & fateor me in explicando primo longiorem fuisse. Sed videtur vir doctus lectis verbis meis aliud quid mente agitasse, quod impedivit quominus ea & recte contraheret, & bene intelligeret. Mentem enim a mea valde alienam mihi affingit. Dixi in exemplo perduellis bona separari posse a conditione sub qua accepta sunt; ille intellexit separari posse ab ipso perduelli, aut a habitu. Itaque aliud dixi, ad aliud ille respondet.
latin.373: Scio bona Adami quibus excidit, potuisse ab eo separari, & separata fuisse. Scio potuisse eorum quaedam a se invicem separari. Scio ea in re similitudinem esse inter Adamum & aulicum perduellem: sed quid hoc ad rhombum? Non enim impedit, esse eam dissimilitudinem inter utrumque quam observavi. Bona enim Adami, hoc est, rectitudo, justitia, integritas, separari non poterant a perfecta obedientia, seu conditione quae ab eo exigebatur. Perseverare in perfecta obedientia erga Deum, & perseverare in rectitudine, justitia, integritate morali, res erant aut eaedem prorsus, aut saltem inseparabiliter connexa: & similiter non perseverare in obedientia erga Deum, & non perseverare in rectitudine, justitia, & integritate, res erant vel eaedem vel indivulse cohaerentes. Num similiter cum fidelitate cohaerent nobilitas, opes, dignitatesque civiles? Num implicat contradictionem illa amissa, has saltem ad tempus retineri? Nonne igitur inter Adamum & eiusmodi perduellem ea in re est memorabilis dissimilitudo?
latin.374: GAR. Deinde, quomodo dicitur in iis quae acciderunt primo homini, nulla opus fuisse judiciaria Dei actione? Annon homini adhuc integro legem Deus proposuerat, de non gustando fructu interdicto, addita gravissima comminatione, si secus faceret, morte moriturum, Gen. 2. 17. Quam comminationem Deus adimplevit, & adimplevit ut judex, ac proinde in spoliando homine suis donis, & in varias miserias demergendo judiciariam actionem exercuit? Hic quoque nihil dissimile.
latin.375: PLAC. Argui, inquam, iam probavi verbis morte morieris non esse intelligendam mortem sitam in privatione justitiae. Quid enim absurdius, quam, aut legem comminari privationem justitiae, aut judicem spoliare eos quos judicat justitia? Probavi etiam Deum illam comminationem legis non adimplevisse in Adamo, ob futuram Christi satisfactionem. Et quomodo potuit adimpleri, si verbis illis mors significabatur corporis & aeterna? punire secundum legis comminationem & non punire: peccatum imputare & non imputare: justificare reum & tamen in eo adimplere legis comminationem, si quid intelligo, ita pugnant, ut consistere simul nequeant. Absit igitur ut credam Deum spoliavisse Adamum justitia originali, ac eum ex justo fecisse injustum.
latin.376: GAR. Neque est quod dicas, hominem eo ipso quod lapsus est, excidisse sua sanctitate & justitia, adeoque nihil opus fuisse actione Dei judiciaria, ut his donis spoliaretur. Quid enim? Non & Regius officiarius, qui bello adversus Regem suscitando, urbe, provincia, Regno excedit, eo ipso excidit illo quod antea gesserat munere: nec tamen eo minus consequenti Regis judicio abdicatur officio suo. PLAC. Omnino excidit munere, hoc est, commeritus est ut munere privetur, idemque munus in alium conferatur: quam ad rem opus est Regis sententia: alioqui non liceret eo munere alium ornare. Censeretur enim is Regius officiarius suum illud munus adhuc retinere. Aliud enim est bellum suscitare, urbe, aut provincia excedere, aliud munere privari: Et sic nonnunquam admisso eiusmodi crimine, ut ad aliquod tempus differatur sententia judiciaria, quo tempore eiusmodi officiarius nondum amisisse suum munus censetur. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Nonne enim ostendi, hoc ipso quod Adamus lapsus est, excidisse eum ex gradu, in quo antea erat, obedientiae & justitiae?
latin.377: Poteratne simul forensi ratione justus & injustus esse? Poteratne simul esse legi Dei conformis & non conformis? perseverare & non perseverare in justitia? Poteratne sese a Deo avertere & incurvare, & tamen rectus permanere? Deum habere pro mendaci, invido, malevolo &c., & tamen conservare amorem, fidem, obedientiam erga Deum, seu justitiam?

pass_a.372: Placeus: if 'separable' means honors can go while riches remain, and affinities while nobility goes, then Adam's goods look separable too—natural light of the intellect, common notions, and the work of the law written on the heart can remain while rectitude, justice, and holiness are lost, as we know happened—and in that the similitude holds again. He grants the four heads were explained in order and that he lingered longest on the first. GAR misread him: Placeus said traitor goods can be separated from the condition under which they were received; GAR heard separated from the traitor himself or from the habit—so one thing said, another answered.
pass_a.373: Placeus knows Adam's lost goods could be and were separated from him, and some from each other, and that this likenesses him to the traitorous courtier—but that misses the point. The dissimilarity he marked remains: Adam's goods (rectitude, justice, integrity) could not be parted from perfect obedience, the required condition. Persevering in obedience and in moral rectitude are the same or inseparably linked; failing either is likewise. Civil nobility, wealth, and dignities do not so cohere with faithfulness that losing faith must lose them at once—a memorable unlikeness.
pass_a.374: GAR next asks how Placeus can say the first man's fall needed no judicial action of God. While man was still integral God set the law not to taste the forbidden fruit with the grave threat dying you shall die (Gen. 2:17). God fulfilled that threat as judge—stripping gifts and plunging into miseries—so here too nothing is unlike the courtier who needs a judge's act.
pass_a.375: Placeus has already proved dying you shall die is not death as privation of justice—absurd for a law to threaten loss of justice, or a judge to strip justice from those he judges. God did not fulfill that legal threat in Adam, because of Christ's future satisfaction. If the words meant bodily and eternal death, punishing and not punishing, imputing and not imputing, justifying the guilty yet fulfilling the threat cannot stand together. So Placeus will not believe God stripped Adam of original justice and made the just man unjust.
pass_a.376: GAR: you cannot say that by the fall itself man dropped holiness and justice so no judicial stripping was needed—a royal officer who raises war against the King and leaves city, province, and realm likewise falls from the office he bore, yet is still formally abdicated by the King's later judgment. Placeus: he altogether deserves deprivation and that the office be conferred on another, which needs the King's sentence—else another cannot lawfully be adorned with it, and the officer would still be held to retain the post. Raising war and leaving a province is not yet being deprived; sometimes the judicial sentence is deferred. But what is that to the point? Adam by falling already left the grade of obedience and justice in which he stood.
pass_a.377: Could Adam at once be forensically just and unjust, conformed and not conformed to God's law, persevering and not persevering in justice? Could he avert and bend from God and still stay upright? Hold God a liar, envious, malevolent, and still keep love, faith, obedience—justice? Tip before GAR's penalties / dying-you-die deepen.

372: PLAC. Perhaps when you say separable, you understand not only that they can be separated—so that, honors being lost, riches can remain, and nobility being lost, affinities can remain. But if it is so explained, who will not retort that Adam's goods also were separable, because the natural light of the intellect, and common notions, and the work of the law written in the hearts could remain, and yet rectitude, justice, holiness be lost—and we know it was done. And in this again the similitude holds. But when the heads of dissimilarity are explained, is nothing said of the first member? I acknowledge the four members were not so proposed by me that they were not explained one by one in order, and I confess I was longer in explaining the first. But the learned man, having read my words, seems to have had something else in mind which hindered him from both rightly contracting them and understanding them well. For he invents for me a mind very alien to mine. I said in the traitor's example that goods can be separated from the condition under which they were received; he understood that they can be separated from the traitor himself, or from the habit. And so I said one thing; he answers another.
373: I know that Adam's goods which he lost could be separated from him, and were separated. I know that some of them could be separated from one another. I know that in that respect there is a likeness between Adam and the traitorous courtier: but what is that to the point? For it does not hinder there being that dissimilarity between them which I observed. For Adam's goods—that is, rectitude, justice, integrity—could not be separated from perfect obedience, or the condition required of him. To persevere in perfect obedience toward God, and to persevere in moral rectitude, justice, integrity, were either altogether the same things, or at least inseparably connected: and likewise not to persevere in obedience toward God, and not to persevere in rectitude, justice, and integrity, were either the same or indivisibly coherent. Do nobility, wealth, and civil dignities cohere similarly with faithfulness? Does it imply a contradiction that, that being lost, these at least for a time be retained? Is there not therefore between Adam and such a traitor a memorable dissimilarity in that respect?
374: GAR. Next, how is it said that in what befell the first man there was no need of God's judicial action? Had not God, while man was still integral, proposed a law of not tasting the forbidden fruit, with the most grave threat added that if he did otherwise he would die the death, Gen. 2:17? Which threat God fulfilled, and fulfilled as judge, and therefore in stripping man of his gifts and plunging him into various miseries exercised a judicial action? Here too there is nothing unlike.
375: PLAC. I argued, I say—I have already proved that by the words dying you shall die is not to be understood a death seated in the privation of justice. For what is more absurd than either that a law should threaten the privation of justice, or that a judge should strip of justice those whom he judges? I have also proved that God did not fulfill that threat of the law in Adam, on account of Christ's future satisfaction. And how could it have been fulfilled, if by those words death of body and eternal death were signified? To punish according to the law's threat and not to punish; to impute sin and not to impute; to justify the guilty and yet in him fulfill the law's threat—if I understand anything—so fight that they cannot stand together. Far be it therefore that I believe God stripped Adam of original justice and made him from just into unjust.
376: GAR. Nor is there room for you to say that man by this very thing—that he fell—fell from his holiness and justice, and so there was no need of God's judicial action to strip him of these gifts. What then? Does not also a royal officer who by raising war against the King leaves city, province, kingdom, by that very thing fall from the office he had formerly borne—and yet is none the less by the King's subsequent judgment abdicated from his office? PLAC. He altogether falls from the office—that is, he has deserved to be deprived of the office, and that the same office be conferred on another: for which the King's sentence is needed; otherwise it would not be lawful to adorn another with that office. For that royal officer would still be held to retain his office. For it is one thing to raise war and leave city or province, another to be deprived of office: and so sometimes, such a crime being committed, the judicial sentence is deferred for some time, during which such an officer is not yet held to have lost his office. But what is this to the matter? Have I not shown that by this very thing—that Adam fell—he fell from the grade of obedience and justice in which he formerly was?
377: Could he at the same time be forensically just and unjust? Could he at the same time be conformed to God's law and not conformed? persevere and not persevere in justice? Could he turn and bend himself away from God and yet remain upright? Hold God for a liar, envious, malevolent, &c., and yet conserve love, faith, obedience toward God—that is, justice?
